name: StrongMinds (charityevals)
summary: StrongMinds treats depression in Uganda and Zambia (and, through partners, Kenya, Malawi and Ethiopia) with six-week group interpersonal therapy run by lay facilitators, most of them government-paid volunteers or former clients. In 2025 it reported 745,224 people treated for $11.4 million, about $15 a person. Taking the bias-corrected effect of psychotherapy for depression in trials outside the West, discounted heavily towards the much smaller effect an independent trial of StrongMinds' model found, the model gives about 0.035 WELLBYs per dollar you give, roughly five times GiveDirectly. The biggest uncertainty is how large and how lasting the effect is at this scale and cost: the charity's own data show very large gains, the one independent RCT a small one that faded within two years. Because effect size, duration and the WELLBY exchange rate all multiply, the joint low–high corners run from below GiveDirectly to over a hundred times it; varying the inputs together over their ranges, the middle 80% of outcomes falls at roughly 2–11 times GiveDirectly.

rows.explainer: All of StrongMinds' 2025 program spending. Almost all of it is the group-therapy program; it also pays for community sensitisation (1.04 million people in 2025), the research and innovations lab, and government technical support, which are not modelled separately. Charging all of it to the people treated is conservative. The US program closed at the end of 2024, so 2025 has no non-African program to exclude. 2025 is the latest year with audited accounts (auditor's report dated June 25, 2026).

People treated for depression, 2025
rows.explainer: StrongMinds' count of people treated in 2025 (the cover page of the same report says 754,224, an apparent typo; the metrics page, the CEO letter and the Q2 2026 report say 745k). It is the charity's administrative count, not independently verified. In 2024 53% of clients were treated through government partners (government-paid volunteer facilitators), 23% by peer facilitators, 21% through NGO partners and 3% by StrongMinds staff; about a third of 2025 clients were adolescents (15–24). Clients start therapy after scoring 10 or more on the PHQ-9 depression questionnaire. Completion and attendance are handled in implementation_adj.

rows.label: Cost per person treated
rows.explainer: About $15, the same as StrongMinds' own 2025 figure (it divides total expenses by people treated). It was $23 in 2024 and $40 in 2023, and $10.55 in the first half of 2026: the fall comes from delivery moving to government-paid volunteers. It excludes the government's own contribution (see attribution_share_shared).

rows.explainer:
The pooled effect of psychotherapy for adult depression against control groups in trials from non-Western countries (105 trials, about 40% of them from low- and lower-middle-income countries), after correcting for publication bias (trim-and-fill), with its 95% CI as the range. Uncorrected the pooled effect is g = 1.10, group formats g = 1.28, low- and lower-middle-income trials g = 1.45 and sub-Saharan African trials g = 1.82; low-risk-of-bias trials give g = 0.69 (0.49–0.89). We start from the bias-corrected figure because the uncorrected effects are implausibly large and the African subgroup is small and noisy. The trials averaged about 9 sessions, and the number of sessions was not associated with the effect.

StrongMinds' own controlled data point higher: its 2026 pilot cluster RCT (StrongMinds authors, preprint) found PHQ-9 scores 7.8 points lower than enhanced usual care at three months (5.2 in the subgroup assessed without facilitators and with an honesty prompt). The one independent RCT of StrongMinds' model (Baird et al. 2024) points much lower; that gap is in evidence_adj.

rows.label: Decay of the effect (SDs per year)
rows.explainer:
How fast the effect fades, assumed linear. 0.3 SD a year makes the 0.6 SD effect last two years. Anchors, all from controlled studies: in Baird et al. (2024), the only independent RCT of StrongMinds' model (adolescent girls in Uganda), the effect per attender on PHQ-8 scores was 0.15 SD at the end of therapy, 0.11 SD at 12 months and nil at 24 months. In StrongMinds' 2019–20 controlled (non-randomised) study, the gap with the control group was 6.2 PHQ-9 points at 6 months and 2.9 at 12 months, as controls recovered on their own. Bass et al. (2006), the 6-month follow-up of Bolton et al.'s Ugandan trial, still found a 14-point gap on a local depression symptom scale. The fast end (0.6 a year, a one-year effect) fits Baird and the halving in the 2019–20 study; the slow end (0.25, about 2.4 years at the central effect) fits a gap that is still present but shrinking at 12 months. We don't use StrongMinds' uncontrolled 12-month follow-up (PHQ-9 still 3.2) to set the slow end, since without a control group it can't separate the treatment from natural recovery.

The benefit is not discounted for time: over a two-year effect the shared discount rate would lower it by only a few percent. The central value was set jointly with evidence_adj, which is calibrated to Baird given this decay.

rows.label: Years until the effect has faded
Total effect per person (SD-years)
rows.explainer: Area of the triangle: linear decay from the initial effect to zero.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person treated
rows.explainer: Converts SD-years of improvement on depression scales into life-satisfaction points with the shared factor (2 WELLBYs per SD-year). As a check, StrongMinds' own 12-month follow-up (no control group) reports clients' life-ladder score rising from 3.1 to 7.5 out of 10, which would be several WELLBYs a year; we don't use it because without a control group it mixes treatment with natural recovery, regression to the mean and wanting to please.

rows.label: Household size
rows.explainer: The shared household size for psychotherapy recipients, measured in Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe: StrongMinds' own countries.

rows.label: Household multiplier (recipient plus spillovers)
rows.explainer: Each other household member is credited with the shared spillover share (about 16%) of the client's own gain. About a third of 2025 clients were adolescents, for whom household spillovers are less studied.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer:
How far the meta-analytic effect should be trusted for StrongMinds at its current scale and cost. The main anchor is Baird et al. (2024), a large independent cluster RCT of StrongMinds Uganda's model delivered by BRAC club mentors to adolescent girls (14 sessions, 2019). Per girl who attended (LATE, Table A4), therapy lowered PHQ-8 scores by 0.73 points (0.15 SD) at the end of therapy and 0.58 points (0.11 SD) at 12 months, with nothing left at 24 months: about 0.19 SD-years. None of these score effects was statistically significant; the significant result was a 5.4-point rise in the share with minimal depression, with gains concentrated around that cutoff, and no effect on moderate or severe depression. Against the model's unadjusted 0.6 SD-years, Baird implies about 0.3.

We set 0.45. After the delivery (0.85) and counterfactual (0.97) adjustments below, which Baird's per-attender estimate already partly reflects, this credits StrongMinds' current adult program with about 1.2 times Baird's per-attender effect (1.5 times before them), because: Baird's clients were adolescents (two thirds of StrongMinds' clients are adults), its 12- and 24-month surveys fell in Uganda's COVID lockdown and the longest school closures in the world, and the program was a first pilot with BRAC. Against going higher: the meta-analysis trials mostly used waitlist or usual-care controls and self-reported symptoms, and StrongMinds' own pilot RCT showed that reports improve when the facilitator is present, a social-desirability bias that inflates both its M&E and many trials; even with that removed, the pilot still found a 5.2-point PHQ-9 gap at three months, which is why we don't go all the way down to Baird. The low end (0.25) takes Baird's per-attender effect at face value with some further loss at scale; the high end (0.9) takes the bias-corrected meta-analysis nearly at face value, as StrongMinds' own controlled studies would support.

This value was set together with the decay rate (0.3 SD a year): Baird anchors the product of effect, duration and this adjustment, so changing the decay without re-deriving this adjustment would count the same evidence twice.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The trial effects are already net of control groups, who recover partly on their own and, in most trials from these countries, received usual care; so natural remission and usual care are not counted again. What remains is whether StrongMinds' clients would otherwise have got psychotherapy that the trials' control groups didn't: the WHO counts about 1.6 mental-health workers per 100,000 people in the African region, so very few would. The 3% (up to 10%) allows for some clients being reached by other psychosocial programs, such as NGO partners' own services or school counselling.

rows.label: StrongMinds' share of credit, when shared with others
rows.explainer: Most clients are now treated by others' staff: 53% (2024) through government partners, whose government-paid volunteers and staff run the groups, and 21% through NGO partners. StrongMinds' own analysis puts government contributions at about 9% of program costs in Uganda and Zambia in 2025 (7–19% in Kenya, ~10% in Malawi), almost all staff time, and calls the figures early. NGO partners appear to pay their own delivery costs: the audited 'Partners' expense line fell from $253,271 in 2024 to $39 in 2025. If the NGO channel's delivery costs per client are similar to StrongMinds' own, partners bear roughly 10–15% of total costs. We credit StrongMinds with its share of all costs: about 9% to governments and about 11% to NGO partners gives 0.8. The low end allows for higher partner costs and volunteers' unpaid time; the high end takes the 2024 estimate of ~5% government contribution and smaller partner costs.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (attendance, dose, reported reach)
rows.explainer: The share of the trial effect that the people counted as treated actually get. Attendance: in routine data on 45,349 clients of the earlier 8-session program (Uganda and Zambia, 2020–21; Assefa et al. 2025) average attendance was 82%, 10% dropped out, and early drop-outs improved by 10.3 PHQ-9 points against 13.3 for full attenders; trial effects are intention-to-treat, so only a shortfall against trial attendance matters (~0.95). Dose: the program is now six sessions, against an average of about 9 in the meta-analysis trials, where the number of sessions was not associated with the effect, and StrongMinds' own trial found six weeks non-inferior to eight (~0.95). Reach: 'treated' is StrongMinds' administrative count across government and partner channels, not independently audited (~0.95). The low end allows for a weaker short course and some over-counting; the high end treats all three as negligible.

rows.label: Funging and leverage
rows.explainer: Would a marginal dollar change what StrongMinds does? Against: it ended 2025 with $14.0 million in cash, more than a year of expenses, after a one-time $5 million grant, so the next dollar may sit in reserves for a while. For: StrongMinds is scaling fast (goal of 1 million clients in 2026), its mid-2026 report shows a 2026 expense budget of $14.2 million, $6.2 million spent in the first half, and $4.5 million of its $12 million fundraising goal still unmet, so reserves are being drawn down; and its government model draws in government staff time that would not otherwise go to depression care. We take 1, with 0.8 if reserves crowd out new money and 1.15 if each dollar pulls in more government resources.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable for-profit jobs
rows.explainer: How much less staff earn than in comparable for-profit roles. Most staff work in Uganda and Zambia, where NGO jobs typically pay at or above comparable local private-sector jobs, so the gap is smaller than the ~15% used for large delivery charities in the repo; US headquarters staff probably take a larger cut. 0 if local NGO pay matches the market; 25% if headquarters pay weighs more than we think.
